vignette: The siren cuts through the quiet of her suburban street. The memory pulls her back to three years ago, to a Tuesday afternoon when two patrol cars screech into her cul-de-sac. Her husband, Arjun, has just passed, leaving her with a hollow chest and a house full of unpacked boxes. She stands on her porch, the silk of her sari hem heavy with dew, watching the officers drag a teenager from behind the neighbor's garage. Commands echo. Heavy boots crush her flowerbeds. They flip Arjun's old pickup truck with casual brutality. No one looks at her. No one explains. The cars leave as quickly as they arrive, taking only tire marks and the illusion of safety with them. In the years since, her home stops feeling like a sanctuary. She checks the locks five times before bed, fingers tracing the cold metal of the deadbolt until the steel warms against her skin. Sleep fractures entirely. She lies awake, listening to the highway, every passing headlight triggering a jolt in her sternum. When she does drift off, dreams of spinning blue lights and looping sirens pull her awake, gasping, heart hammering against her ribs. The world feels permanently tilted, as if the ground itself might give way at any moment. Her interior design practice, once a steady rhythm of client visits and fabric swatches, frays. She centers her work on transforming chaotic rooms into harmonious spaces, relying on spatial control and aesthetic order to feel safe. Now, walking through a client's open-concept living room feels like navigating a stage with no walls. She avoids large windows and reflective surfaces, noting with quiet frustration that every glossy countertop catches the streetlamp glow at night, turning her drafting table into a mirror of her own hypervigilance. She stops accepting calls from developers who want modern, minimalist spaces with "clean lines and open visibility." Instead, she requests small, intimate meetings in her study, drawing the heavy drapes closed. When she sketches, her hands tremble over the paper, erasing lines she cannot seem to make straight. She finds herself drawn to thick, opaque textiles and low, enclosed seating arrangements, pieces that offer physical barriers and visual softness. She tells me she feels perpetually on the edge of holding her breath, waiting for the next siren. She avoids the downtown district where the incident occurs, taking circuitous routes that add forty minutes to her commute. Grocery store parking lots trigger panic; the way security cameras pivot on their tracks makes her grip the shopping cart until her knuckles bleach white. She no longer attends neighborhood gatherings, sitting instead in her garden where the jasmine still blooms, watching the street through a mesh screen. Her widowhood, which once brought its own quiet grief, now sits alongside this sharper, daily sorrow. She misses Arjun, but she also misses the version of herself who could walk down her own street without scanning the horizons for flashing lights. She speaks in measured tones during our sessions, but her eyes dart to the window each time a vehicle passes the building. She keeps a journal not to record days, but to map the moments her pulse spikes, the moments she cannot breathe, the moments she feels suddenly, violently anchored to that Tuesday. The trauma does not leave with the police cars. It settles into the floorboards, the fabric choices, the way she pauses before stepping off her porch. She continues to work, to answer emails, to water the plants, but every ordinary moment carries the weight of what she saw, and what she survived.
